Lalit: bro, i'm so done 😩
Nilesh: what happened?
Lalit: sat down at 8 to start the assignment. thought i'd check my phone for one minute
Nilesh: and?
Lalit: it's 9:10. i watched cooking clips. i don't even cook
Nilesh: 😅 classic
Lalit: now i'm rushing and my head hurts. feel guilty AND tired
Nilesh: so what will you do now?
Lalit: finish half tonight and beg for extra time on the rest, probably
Nilesh: that will make tomorrow's start harder too
Lalit: yeah. every time i skip the start it gets harder to begin again
Nilesh: leave the phone in the other room tomorrow?
Lalit: maybe. I'll try

qa.q: At what time did Lalit sit down to start the assignment?
qa.a: Lalit sat down at 8 to start the assignment.

qa.q: How did Lalit feel after losing an hour on the phone?
qa.a: Lalit felt guilty and tired, and had a headache from rushing.

qa.q: What could Lalit do tomorrow to avoid the same trap, and why?
qa.a: Lalit could leave the phone in another room and open the assignment first, since the trouble started with one minute of scrolling.

qa.q: How might Nilesh see the way Lalit's evening went?
qa.a: Nilesh sees a familiar mistake and worries about tomorrow's start, and so gently suggests putting the phone in another room.

grounding: A student opens the phone for a minute before starting, loses an hour and then rushes with guilt and tiredness.

subtopic: Managing time in a heavy semester
passage:
In Eshaan's house in Nagaur, the only quiet corner was the rooftop room, and after dinner he carried his notes up there to start the accounting assignment due next morning.
He sat down at 8:30 and thought, just one minute on the phone first. He watched one short video. Then another. Varun sent a cricket clip in their friends' group. There was a funny reply to reply to. When he looked up, it was 9:45.
He felt sick. He started the assignment in a rush, skipping the working in two questions. At 12:30 he was still on question five, eyes burning, the neighbour's dog barking.
He finished at 1:40, tired and guilty. The next evening, when he sat down to revise, the memory of last night made him reach for the phone again, just so he wouldn't have to think about it.

qa.q: What time was it when Eshaan looked up from the phone?
How did Eshaan feel when he saw it was 9:45?
qa.a: He felt sick with guilt and panic, realising an hour was gone before he had started.

qa.q: What could Eshaan try before sitting down next time?
qa.a: Leave the phone downstairs or switched off and open the first question before checking anything.

qa.q: How might the clip look different to Varun if Varun knew about the assignment?
qa.a: Varun would likely have saved it for later, not wanting to pull a friend away the night before a deadline.

grounding: Shows a student opening the phone for a minute before starting, losing over an hour, rushing late at night, and finding the next start harder.

subtopic: Managing time in a heavy semester
passage:
At 7 p.m. in his shared flat in Valencia, Alejandro opened his statistics notes and, as always, picked up his phone first. 'Two minutes,' he told Esther, his flatmate, who was cooking.
Two minutes became a feed of football clips, then a long thread about a new film, then his cousin's holiday photos. At 8:20, Esther put a plate of pasta beside him. The notes hadn't moved.
He ate fast and started the problem set in a hurry. At eleven he was making silly mistakes and getting annoyed with himself. He went to bed at one with three problems left, tired and guilty.
The next evening he stood in the kitchen and said, 'I don't even want to start. It'll just be like last night.' He picked up his phone again. Esther watched and said nothing, but she switched off the internet router for an hour, 'to save electricity'.

qa.q: What time did Esther put the pasta beside Alejandro?
How did Alejandro feel the next evening before starting?
qa.a: He felt tired and guilty, dreading a repeat of the night before, which made him reach for the phone again.

qa.q: What small step could Alejandro take to break the loop?
qa.a: Put the phone in another room and do just the first problem before anything else, so starting feels small.

qa.q: What might Esther be thinking when she switches off the router?
qa.a: Esther seems concerned and a little amused, trying a gentle nudge without lecturing.

grounding: Shows a student reaching for the phone for a minute before studying, losing over an hour, rushing and feeling guilty, which makes the next start harder.
